title: Chapter 6 — What Sort Of Despotism Democratic Nations Have To Fear
paragraphs: While I was in the United States, I noticed that a democratic state of society like the Americans’ might offer unusual openings for establishing despotism. After I returned to Europe, I saw how much most of our rulers had already exploited the ideas, feelings, and needs that this same social condition produces, in order to widen the reach of their power. This made me think that the nations of Christendom might in time suffer some kind of oppression like the one that once weighed on several nations of the ancient world. I have examined the subject more closely and thought about it for five more years. My fears have not lessened, but they now point at a different object. In earlier ages, no sovereign was ever so absolute or so powerful that he tried to administer every part of a great empire by his own agency, without intermediate powers to help him. None ever tried to bind all his subjects, without distinction, to a strict uniformity of regulation, or to tutor and direct each member of the community in person. Such an undertaking never occurred to the human mind. And had anyone conceived it, the lack of information, the flaws of the administrative system, and above all the natural obstacles that the inequality of conditions created would soon have stopped so vast a design from being carried out. When the Roman emperors were at the height of their power, the different nations of the empire kept very diverse customs and ways of life. Though all were subject to the same monarch, most of the provinces were administered separately, and they were full of strong and active municipalities. And although the whole government of the empire was concentrated in the emperor’s hands, and he remained, on occasion, the final arbiter in every matter, the details of social life and of private occupations were for the most part beyond his control. It is true that the emperors held an immense and unchecked power, which let them indulge every whim and use the whole strength of the state for that purpose. They often abused this power arbitrarily, taking away their subjects’ property or lives. Their tyranny weighed very heavily on a few people, but it did not reach the majority. It fixed on a handful of main objects and ignored the rest; it was violent, but its range was limited.

But it seems that if despotism were ever established among the democratic nations of our day, it would have a different character. It would be wider in extent and milder in manner; it would degrade men without tormenting them. I do not doubt that in an age of education and equality like ours, sovereigns could more easily gather all political power into their own hands, and could intrude more regularly and more forcefully into the sphere of private interests, than any sovereign of antiquity ever could. Yet the very principle of equality that makes despotism easier also softens its harshness. We have seen that the customs of a society grow more humane and gentle as men become more equal and more alike. When no member of the community has great power or great wealth, tyranny has, so to speak, no openings and no ground to work on. Since every fortune is modest, people’s passions are naturally confined, their imaginations are limited, and their pleasures are simple. This universal moderation moderates the sovereign too, and holds the excessive reach of his desires within certain bounds.

Apart from these reasons, which come from the nature of the social state itself, I could add many others that arise from causes outside my subject, but I will stay within the limits I have set for myself. Democratic governments may turn violent and even cruel in times of extreme agitation or great danger, but such crises will be rare and short. When I consider the petty passions of our contemporaries, the mildness of their customs, the breadth of their education, the purity of their religion, the gentleness of their morality, their orderly and hardworking habits, and the restraint that almost all of them show in their vices as well as in their virtues, I have no fear that they will find tyrants in their rulers, but rather guardians. *a I think, then, that the kind of oppression threatening democratic nations is unlike anything that has existed in the world before; our contemporaries will find no precedent for it in their memories. I am trying to find a word that would convey the whole idea I have formed of it, but I try in vain. The old words “despotism” and “tyranny” do not fit; the thing itself is new, and since I cannot name it, I must try to define it.

I want to trace the new features under which despotism might appear in the world. The first thing that strikes the observer is an innumerable crowd of men, all equal and alike, constantly striving to win the small and trivial pleasures that fill their lives. Each of them, living apart, is like a stranger to the fate of all the others. His children and his close friends make up the whole of mankind for him. As for his other fellow citizens, he stands beside them but does not see them; he touches them but does not feel them. He exists only in himself and for himself alone; and if he still has his family, he can at least be said to have lost his country. Above this crowd stands an immense and protective power, which takes on the sole task of securing their enjoyments and watching over their fate. That power is absolute, detailed, regular, farsighted, and mild. It would resemble parental authority if, like that authority, its aim were to prepare men for adulthood. But it seeks instead to keep them in permanent childhood. It is quite content for the people to enjoy themselves, so long as they think of nothing but enjoyment. Such a government works willingly for their happiness, but it insists on being the only agent and sole judge of that happiness. It provides for their security, foresees and supplies their needs, makes their pleasures easier, manages their main concerns, directs their industry, regulates the passing down of property, and divides up their inheritances. What is left, except to spare them the effort of thinking and the trouble of living? In this way it makes the use of free will less useful and less frequent every day. It confines the will within a narrower range and gradually strips each man of the use of himself. The principle of equality has readied men for all this: it has inclined them to put up with it, and often even to see it as a benefit.

Once the supreme power has taken each member of the community in its strong grip in turn and shaped each one as it pleases, it stretches its arm over the whole community. It covers the surface of society with a web of small, intricate rules, detailed and uniform, which even the most original minds and the most energetic characters cannot break through to rise above the crowd. The will of man is not shattered but softened, bent, and guided. Men are seldom forced to act, but they are constantly held back from acting. Such a power does not destroy; it prevents things from coming into being. It does not tyrannize; it compresses, weakens, extinguishes, and dulls a people, until each nation is reduced to nothing better than a flock of timid, hardworking animals with the government as its shepherd. I have always believed that servitude of the regular, quiet, and gentle kind I have just described could be combined more easily than people commonly think with some of the outward forms of freedom, and that it could even take root under the wing of the sovereignty of the people. Our contemporaries are constantly pulled by two conflicting passions: they want to be led, and they want to remain free. Since they cannot destroy either of these opposing inclinations, they try to satisfy both at once. They imagine a single, protective, all-powerful government, but one chosen by the people. They combine centralization with the sovereignty of the people. This gives them some relief. They console themselves for being under guardianship by reflecting that they chose their own guardians. Each man lets himself be put in leading-strings because he sees that it is not a person or a class but the people as a whole who hold the end of his chain. Under this system the people throw off their dependence just long enough to choose a master, and then fall back into it. A great many people today are quite content with this sort of compromise between administrative despotism and the sovereignty of the people, and they think they have done enough to protect individual freedom once they have handed it over to the power of the nation at large. That does not satisfy me. It matters less to me who the master is that I must obey than that obedience is being extorted from me.

I do not deny, however, that a constitution of this kind seems to me infinitely better than one that would concentrate all the powers of government and then place them in the hands of an irresponsible person or body. Of all the forms democratic despotism could take, the latter would certainly be the worst. When the sovereign is elected, or is closely watched by a legislature that is truly elected and independent, the oppression he exerts over individuals is sometimes heavier, but it is always less degrading. For each man, even while oppressed and disarmed, can still imagine that in obeying he is obeying himself, and that all his other wishes are yielding to one of his own inclinations. In the same way, I can see that when the sovereign represents the nation and depends on the people, the rights and power taken from every citizen serve not only the head of state but the state itself, and individuals get something back in return for the independence they have given up to the public. So to create a representation of the people in every centralized country is to reduce the evil that extreme centralization can produce, but not to be rid of it. I grant that this leaves room for individuals to take part in the more important affairs, but their intervention is no less suppressed in the smaller and more private ones. We must not forget that it is especially dangerous to enslave men in the small details of life. For my part, I would be inclined to think that freedom matters less in great things than in small ones, if one could be sure of having the former without the latter. Subjection in small matters shows itself every day and is felt by the whole community without distinction. It does not drive men to resist, but it thwarts them at every turn, until they give up using their will at all. In this way their spirit is gradually broken and their character weakened. Obedience demanded only on a few important but rare occasions, by contrast, shows servitude only at intervals and puts its burden on a small number of men. It is pointless to call on a people made so dependent on the central power to choose that power’s representatives from time to time. This rare and brief use of their free choice, however important, will not stop them from gradually losing the ability to think, feel, and act for themselves, and so from sinking gradually below the level of humanity. *b I add that they will soon be unable to use the great and only privilege that remains to them. The democratic nations that introduced freedom into their political constitution at the very moment they were increasing the despotism of their administrative constitution have been led into strange contradictions. For managing small affairs, where plain good sense is all that is needed, the people are judged unequal to the task. Yet when the government of the country is at stake, the people are given immense powers. They are made, by turns, the playthings of their ruler and his masters — more than kings, and less than men. After trying every method of election without finding one that suits them, they are still astonished and still determined to look further, as if the evil they notice came far more from the constitution of the country than from that of the electoral body. It is indeed hard to see how men who have entirely given up the habit of governing themselves could succeed in choosing well those who are to govern them. And no one will ever believe that a liberal, wise, and energetic government can come from the votes of a subservient people. A constitution that was republican at its head and ultra-monarchical in all its other parts has always seemed to me a short-lived monster. The vices of the rulers and the ineptitude of the people would soon bring about its ruin. The nation, tired of its representatives and of itself, would then create freer institutions, or before long return to stretch itself out at the feet of a single master.
